bodyText:
Introduction to Data Structures

A data structure is a systematic way of organizing, storing and managing data in a computer so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently. The choice of data structure affects the time and memory required by an algorithm. Data structures are broadly classified as linear and non-linear. Linear structures arrange data in a sequence, while non-linear structures arrange data hierarchically or in a network.

Arrays

An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations. Each element is identified by an index, usually starting from 0 in most programming languages such as C, C++ and Java. The address of an element can be computed directly from the base address and the index, which makes random access very fast.

Arrays have a fixed size once declared, although dynamic arrays in some languages can resize. Insertion and deletion in the middle of an array are expensive because the remaining elements must be shifted. The main advantages of arrays are fast access by index and simplicity; the main disadvantages are fixed size and costly insertion and deletion.

Linked Lists

A linked list is a linear data structure in which elements, called nodes, are stored in non-contiguous memory locations. Each node contains data and a pointer (or link) to the next node. The first node is called the head, and the last node points to NULL, indicating the end of the list.

There are three common types of linked lists. A singly linked list has one pointer per node, pointing to the next node. A doubly linked list has two pointers per node, one to the next node and one to the previous node, allowing traversal in both directions. A circular linked list has its last node pointing back to the first node, forming a loop.

Linked lists allow insertion and deletion at any position without shifting elements, because only pointers need to be updated. However, accessing an element requires traversing the list from the head, so random access is not possible. Linked lists use extra memory for pointers, but they can grow and shrink dynamically at run time.

Arrays versus Linked Lists

Arrays store elements in contiguous memory and allow direct access by index, while linked lists store elements in scattered memory and require sequential traversal. Arrays have a fixed size and costly insertion and deletion, whereas linked lists are dynamic and allow efficient insertion and deletion once the position is found. Arrays use less memory per element because no pointers are stored, but they may waste memory if the allocated size is larger than needed.
keyPoints: A data structure is a systematic way of organizing, storing and managing data so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently.
An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored in contiguous memory locations.
In most languages such as C, C++ and Java, array indexing starts from 0.
Accessing an element of an array by index takes O(1) time, also called constant time.
Insertion or deletion in the middle of an array takes O(n) time because elements must be shifted.
A linked list is a linear data structure in which each node contains data and a pointer to the next node.
The first node of a linked list is called the head, and the last node points to NULL.
A singly linked list has one pointer per node; a doubly linked list has pointers to both the next and the previous node.
A circular linked list has its last node pointing back to the first node.
Insertion and deletion in a linked list take O(1) time once the position is reached, because only pointers are updated.
Searching for an element in a linked list takes O(n) time because traversal starts from the head.
Arrays use less memory per element than linked lists because linked lists store an extra pointer in every node.

bodyText:
Stacks

A stack is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO principle, which stands for Last In, First Out. The element inserted last is the first one to be removed. A stack has one open end, called the top. The two basic operations are push, which inserts an element onto the top, and pop, which removes the element from the top. The peek operation returns the top element without removing it.

A stack can be implemented using an array or a linked list. Common applications include function call management in program execution, undo operations in text editors, backtracking in algorithms, and the evaluation of arithmetic expressions. When a function is called, its return address and local variables are stored in a stack frame on the call stack.

Queues

A queue is a linear data structure that follows the FIFO principle, which stands for First In, First Out. The element inserted first is the first one to be removed. A queue has two ends: elements are inserted at the rear and removed from the front. The basic operations are enqueue, which inserts an element at the rear, and dequeue, which removes an element from the front.

Common applications of queues include print job scheduling, process scheduling in operating systems, breadth-first search in graphs, and buffering in data communication. A circular queue reuses the empty spaces at the front of the array by wrapping the rear pointer back to the start. A priority queue removes the element with the highest priority first, rather than the element that arrived first. A double-ended queue, or deque, allows insertion and deletion at both ends.

Expression Notation

Stacks are used to convert and evaluate arithmetic expressions. In infix notation, the operator is written between the operands, for example A + B. In prefix notation, also called Polish notation, the operator comes before the operands, for example + A B. In postfix notation, also called Reverse Polish notation, the operator comes after the operands, for example A B +. Polish notation was introduced by the Polish logician Jan Lukasiewicz in the 1920s. Postfix expressions are evaluated using a stack: operands are pushed, and when an operator is met, two operands are popped, the operation is performed, and the result is pushed back.
keyPoints: LIFO stands for Last In, First Out, the principle followed by a stack.
FIFO stands for First In, First Out, the principle followed by a queue.
Push inserts an element onto the top of a stack, and pop removes the element from the top of a stack.
Enqueue inserts an element at the rear of a queue, and dequeue removes an element from the front of a queue.
Both push and pop on a stack take O(1) time, and both enqueue and dequeue on a queue take O(1) time.
A stack overflow occurs when a push is attempted on a full stack, and a stack underflow occurs when a pop is attempted on an empty stack.
Function calls are managed using a stack, called the call stack, which stores return addresses and local variables.
A circular queue reuses empty spaces at the front of the array by wrapping the rear pointer back to the start.
A priority queue removes the element with the highest priority first, not necessarily the element that arrived first.
A deque, or double-ended queue, allows insertion and deletion at both ends.
Infix notation writes the operator between operands, for example A + B; postfix notation writes it after them, for example A B +.
Polish notation was introduced by the Polish logician Jan Lukasiewicz in the 1920s.

bodyText:
Introduction to Trees

A tree is a non-linear, hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges. The topmost node is called the root. Every node except the root has exactly one parent, and a node may have zero or more children. A node with no children is called a leaf node. The depth of a node is the number of edges from the root to that node, and the height of a tree is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf. A tree with n nodes always has n minus 1 edges.

Binary Trees

A binary tree is a tree in which each node has at most two children, called the left child and the right child. A full binary tree is one in which every node has either zero or two children. A complete binary tree is one in which all levels are completely filled except possibly the last, which is filled from left to right. A perfect binary tree is one in which all internal nodes have two children and all leaves are at the same level. A binary tree of height h has at most 2 to the power h plus 1, minus 1 nodes.

There are three standard ways to traverse a binary tree. Inorder traversal visits the left subtree, then the root, then the right subtree. Preorder traversal visits the root first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree. Postorder traversal visits the left subtree, then the right subtree, then the root. Traversal of a binary tree takes O(n) time, where n is the number of nodes.

Binary Search Trees

A binary search tree, abbreviated BST, is a binary tree with a special ordering property: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller than the node's value, and all values in its right subtree are greater than the node's value. This property makes searching efficient, because at each step roughly half of the remaining tree can be discarded.

To insert a value into a BST, start at the root and compare the value with each node: go left if the value is smaller and right if it is greater, until an empty position is reached, then place the new node there. To search for a value, start at the root and follow the same left or right choices until the value is found or an empty position is reached, which means the value is absent. For example, inserting 50, 30, 70, 20 and 40 in that order gives 50 as the root, 30 as its left child, 70 as its right child, 20 as the left child of 30, and 40 as the right child of 30. Searching for 40 then visits 50, 30 and 40, in that order.

An important property of a BST is that an inorder traversal visits the nodes in ascending sorted order. In a balanced BST, search, insertion and deletion each take O(log n) time on average. In the worst case, when values are inserted in sorted order, the BST degenerates into a chain, and these operations take O(n) time. Self-balancing trees such as AVL trees and red-black trees avoid this by keeping the height logarithmic.
keyPoints: BST stands for Binary Search Tree, a binary tree with an ordering property on its values.
A tree with n nodes always has n minus 1 edges.
The topmost node of a tree is called the root, and a node with no children is called a leaf node.
In a binary tree, each node has at most two children: a left child and a right child.
In a BST, all values in the left subtree are smaller than the node's value, and all values in the right subtree are greater.
Inorder traversal visits left subtree, root, right subtree; preorder visits root, left, right; postorder visits left, right, root.
An inorder traversal of a BST visits the nodes in ascending sorted order.
In a balanced BST, search, insertion and deletion take O(log n) time on average.
In the worst case, a BST degenerates into a chain and search, insertion and deletion take O(n) time.
A binary tree of height h has at most 2 to the power (h + 1), minus 1 nodes.
Traversing a binary tree visits every node once, so traversal takes O(n) time.
AVL trees and red-black trees are self-balancing trees that keep the height logarithmic to avoid degeneration.

bodyText:
What Sorting Means

Sorting is the process of arranging data in a particular order, usually ascending or descending. A sorting algorithm is said to be stable if it preserves the relative order of equal elements. An in-place sorting algorithm sorts using only a constant amount of extra memory, apart from the input itself. Sorting is one of the most frequently tested topics in computer science examinations, and candidates are expected to know the working, the time complexity and the best or worst cases of the standard algorithms.

Bubble Sort: Worked Example

Bubble sort repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. After each pass, the largest unsorted element bubbles up to its correct position at the end. Consider the array 5, 2, 4, 1. Pass 1: compare 5 and 2, swap to get 2, 5, 4, 1; compare 5 and 4, swap to get 2, 4, 5, 1; compare 5 and 1, swap to get 2, 4, 1, 5. Pass 2: compare 2 and 4, no swap; compare 4 and 1, swap to get 2, 1, 4, 5. Pass 3: compare 2 and 1, swap to get 1, 2, 4, 5. The array is now sorted. Bubble sort is simple but slow, and it is stable and in-place.

Selection Sort: Worked Example

Selection sort divides the array into a sorted part and an unsorted part. In each pass, it finds the smallest element in the unsorted part and swaps it with the first element of the unsorted part. Consider the array 5, 2, 4, 1. Pass 1: the smallest element is 1, swap it with 5 to get 1, 2, 4, 5. Pass 2: the smallest of the remaining part is 2, already in place. Pass 3: the smallest of the remaining part is 4, already in place. The array is sorted after only one actual swap. Selection sort always performs the same number of comparisons regardless of the input order, and it is in-place but not stable.

Merge Sort: Worked Example

Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm: it divides the array into halves, sorts each half recursively, and then merges the sorted halves back together. Consider the array 5, 2, 4, 1. Divide it into 5, 2 and 4, 1, then into single elements 5, 2, 4, 1. Merge 5 and 2 into 2, 5, and merge 4 and 1 into 1, 4. Finally merge 2, 5 and 1, 4: compare 2 and 1, take 1; compare 2 and 4, take 2; compare 5 and 4, take 4; take 5, giving 1, 2, 4, 5. Merge sort is stable, but it is not in-place because merging requires extra memory proportional to the size of the array.
keyPoints: Sorting is the process of arranging data in ascending or descending order.
A stable sorting algorithm preserves the relative order of equal elements.
An in-place sorting algorithm uses only a constant amount of extra memory apart from the input.
Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.
Bubble sort has worst-case and average-case time complexity O(n squared) and best-case complexity O(n) when the input is already sorted and an early-exit check is used.
Bubble sort is stable and in-place.
Selection sort finds the smallest element in the unsorted part in each pass and swaps it into place.
Selection sort has time complexity O(n squared) in the best, average and worst cases.
Selection sort is in-place but not stable.
Selection sort performs at most n minus 1 swaps, which makes it useful when swaps are expensive.
Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that divides, sorts recursively, and merges the sorted halves.
Merge sort has time complexity O(n log n) in the best, average and worst cases, and it is stable but not in-place, requiring O(n) extra space.

bodyText:
What Searching Means

Searching is the process of finding a particular element, called the target or key, in a collection of data. If the element is found, the search returns its position; if it is not found, the search reports failure. The two standard searching algorithms are linear search and binary search, and the choice between them depends mainly on whether the data is sorted.

Linear Search

Linear search, also called sequential search, checks each element of the collection one by one, from the first to the last, until the target is found or the end is reached. It works on both sorted and unsorted data and requires no preparation of the data. Its main drawback is speed: in the worst case it must examine every element. Linear search takes O(1) time in the best case, when the target is the first element, and O(n) time in the worst and average cases, where n is the number of elements.

Binary Search: Step-by-Step Example

Binary search works only on sorted data. It repeatedly divides the search interval in half: it compares the target with the middle element, and if the target is smaller it continues in the left half, if larger it continues in the right half, and if equal the search ends successfully. Consider the sorted array 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56 and the target 23. Step 1: the middle of the whole array is 12, and 23 is greater than 12, so search the right half 16, 23, 38, 56. Step 2: the middle of this half is 23, which equals the target, so the search ends successfully at that position. Only two comparisons were needed, whereas linear search would have needed six.

Binary search takes O(log n) time in the worst and average cases, which is dramatically faster than linear search for large data sets. For example, searching one million sorted elements needs at most about 20 comparisons with binary search, compared with up to one million with linear search. Binary search can be implemented iteratively with a loop or recursively by calling itself on the smaller half.
keyPoints: Searching is the process of finding a target element, called the key, in a collection of data.
Linear search, also called sequential search, checks each element one by one from first to last.
Linear search works on both sorted and unsorted data and needs no preparation of the data.
Linear search takes O(1) time in the best case and O(n) time in the worst and average cases.
Binary search works only on sorted data.
Binary search repeatedly compares the target with the middle element and discards half of the remaining data at each step.
Binary search takes O(log n) time in the worst and average cases.
Binary search takes O(1) time in the best case, when the target is the middle element on the first comparison.
Searching one million sorted elements needs at most about 20 comparisons with binary search, since 2 to the power 20 is about one million.
Binary search can be implemented iteratively with a loop or recursively by calling itself on the smaller half.
If the data is unsorted, it must first be sorted before binary search can be applied, which adds the cost of sorting.
For small or unsorted data sets, linear search is simpler and often preferable despite its O(n) time.
